current_answer: People have built games, browser demos, desktop apps, art, brain engines and research tests on real fruit fly connectomes, mainly FlyWire (female brain) and MaleCNS (male brain and nerve cord). We checked 152 of them on 15 October 2026: 50 can be opened in a browser or free notebook without installing anything (in our browser checks of 3, 6 and 11 Oct 2026, 9 of 12 demos ran on a machine without a GPU). Is it a brain or just a map? It is a map of one fly's wiring (a fly brain scan) run with a simple neuron model, and in our own pre-registered tests that wiring made a difference. What the map leaves out: The model is one fly's wiring map: 138,639 neurons and 15,091,983 connections, run with one simple neuron rule. It leaves out electrical synapses (gap junctions), neuropeptides, learning, the different behaviour of different kinds of neurons (including neurons that do not spike), the differences between flies and over a fly's life, and the nerve cord and body. So it can show what the wiring alone does, not everything a fly's brain does. (one number and one source per part: https://shaduf.ai/p/digital-fly-catalog/how-it-works/#missing-heading) We ran the map. A looming shadow on one eye turned our simulated fly away in 6 of 6 runs. With the same map scrambled (same number of connections per neuron) it turned away in 0 of 3. Here the map's wiring, not the stimulus or our code, makes the turn. (5 and 8 Oct 2026; left eye 3 of 3, right eye 3 of 3; the body walks with FlyGym's own controller through our hand-made mapping.) With the escape neuron silenced, the fly still turned away. With only the inside of the map scrambled, the fly turned away in 0 of 6 runs. In brain-only follow-ups: We turned the scrambled maps up until they were as busy as the real one. They still did not produce the turn: the wiring, not the amount of activity, makes it. (6 Oct) How strong must the shadow be? (8 Oct) We lowered the input to the looming neurons step by step, from 80 to 10 spikes per second each. The turn command appeared from about 30 per second (38% of our strongest input) on both sides; below that the model did not turn. The escape neuron started firing at the same input as the turn command. A second random seed agreed. Caveat: One model (Shiu et al. LIF on FlyWire v783), brain only; the input is a rate we set for every LC4/LPLC2 of one eye, not a measured response to a real shadow; 'silenced' means the neuron's output synapses were removed; not a real fly. Which relays carry the turn? (9 Oct, read by firing rate): silencing the relays lowered the turn command to about 60-70% of normal, but silencing random active neurons also moved it, so this is not yet specific to the relays. Silencing other active neurons also changed the turn command, so this relay result is not specific to the relay neurons. With one relay neuron (PVLP141) silenced, the turn command fell to about 70% (left eye) / 65% (right eye) of normal (3 runs per eye). With the 17 (left eye) / 20 (right eye) relay neurons that excite the turn neuron silenced, the turn command fell to about 65% (left eye) / 60% (right eye) of normal (3 runs per eye). The left eye's normal range is only 1 Hz wide (24-25 Hz) and the random control is one draw per eye. One model (Shiu et al. LIF on FlyWire v783), brain only; the input is a rate we set for every LC4/LPLC2 of one eye, not a measured response to a real shadow; 'silenced' means the neuron's output synapses were removed; the normal range comes from 3 runs per eye; not a real fly. On 8 Oct, by the left/right contrast: With one relay neuron (PVLP141) silenced, the turn command stayed (by the left/right contrast (8 Oct)). We found no measured real-fly LC4/LPLC2 firing rate to compare against. A coupled brain-and-body test is not yet tested. The 'away' direction rests on our mapping and fly67's claim. Against an activity-matched control (13 Oct, pre-registered, brain only): The two sides disagree: on one side silencing the relays lowered the turn neuron's rate more than matched activity elsewhere, on the other it did not. We do not draw a conclusion. 15 Oct: we ran 5 more matched controls on the right side, 10 in all. Every one of them left the turn neuron's rate higher than silencing the relays did (controls 38-47 Hz, relays 25.7 Hz), so the right-side reading did not change. Our rule compares the relays with the lowest matched control, so extra controls can only make the relays look less special, never more. (5 seeds per side; 5 matched draws on the left and 10 on the right; some matched draws include direct inputs to the turn neuron; E2 is mostly PVLP141; the 9 Oct random control removed 2-6 times as much activity.) The looming turn in degrees, at each input strength (14 Oct, pre-registered, simulated body): left eye: In the body, the fly turned away from 30 spikes/s per looming neuron upward on this side, the strength at which the brain's turn command appeared; the turn was about 11 deg at 30 and about 37 deg at 80 (our mapping turns the brain's rates into steering). Right eye: At 30 spikes/s the turn was borderline: the fly turned away in 1 of 2 runs on this side; from 40 upward it turned away in every run. The right-eye borderline rests on one run: seed 0 at 30 spikes/s turned 9.18 deg beyond the no-brain floor, against the 10 deg rule. These body runs turn the brain's firing rates into steering through our own hand-made mapping, so they show the brain result in degrees; they are not a separate test of the wiring. No scrambled brains were run at these strengths. Does the real wiring layout help a trained fly vision model (flyvis) see which way things move? (made by us, tried on 10 and 12 Oct 2026) Not decided: a second, lower-memory attempt on 12 Oct also needed more memory than our shared machine has (about 3 GB at its peak; the machine allows 3 GB for everything running on it). The first attempt on 10 Oct also stopped for memory. We did not retrain the model after shuffling. A model trained on the shuffled wiring might do better, so this asks a narrower question: does this trained model depend on the real layout? Is it AI? The base model is not trained AI: it copies the wiring and sets one strength by hand; of 117 graded projects, 69 add a trained, learning or search-tuned part in the main path (catalogue field trained_class). Can it learn? Some projects say so. By our reading of 13 of them, practice changes a trained readout (3), trained settings across the network (4) or a learning rule on some connections (3); 1 trains nothing; 2 give no code. 3 compare with scrambled wiring. Can it suffer? We found no study that measured consciousness or suffering in these models; fly larvae detect harmful heat and pressure, and whether flies feel pain is open. Can I put it in my game? Yes for a non-commercial project with credit, in our cautious reading of FlyWire's CC BY-NC 4.0 (its Zenodo record says CC BY 4.0; not legal advice); MaleCNS is CC BY 4.0. What do I have to download? Two files, 104.1 MB, to run the brain model; FlyWire v783 in full is 10.6 GB, MaleCNS 31.3 GB, BANC 536.1 GB. Most viral demos really run a simulated fly brain, but a person chose which neurons receive the input and which neurons act, and several get most of their movement from scripts or trained parts; no fly has been "uploaded". The graded claim "Can A Conscious Fly Brain Learn how to Hack?" by dzuma (approximately 72,728 views on 12 Oct 2026, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m5Q_aIO_K8o) links no code and is graded U; on 15 Oct 2026 the repositories of 14 of the 22 verdict rows were re-checked (14 with code unchanged since graded, 8 with no code). Does the real fly wiring help? Sometimes: across 58 control studies it beat scrambled wiring in 22 of 49, mostly untrained reflex, sensory and steering circuits; in trained, reservoir, ML, game, robot-arm and our walking tests it tied or lost (14). Across 27 studies with a no-brain baseline the fly network beats it in only 4; in Doom a brainless autopilot survives 51.93 s against the fly brain's 53.34 s (doom-fly-control by gabrycina), and in our walking test a scrambled brain and no brain walked the FlyGym fly as far as the real brain. A beginner can run the published whole-brain model on a CPU: in our test on 2 CPUs sugar input drove MN9 to 85.2 Hz and shuffled wiring dropped it to 0 Hz; re-tested 5 Oct 2026 (6 of 6 tests, 82.0 Hz bit-exact), with tested deeper steps for a FlyGym body and a looming sense. Brain (Brian2 2.9.0) and body (FlyGym 2.1.0) installed together in one Python 3.12 environment: 1.1 GB on disk, tested 8 Oct 2026, with numpy pinned to 2.3.5 (Brian2 2.9.0 does not import with numpy 2.5.3). A 20-minute Use in class plan is on Build your own.

catalogue_card.question: What have people built with the digital fruit fly brain, and what is real?
catalogue_card.text: 152 fruit fly brain simulation projects checked in code, each marked for trained parts (is it AI?): 50 you can try online, 56 videos with evidence grades, verdicts on 22 viral claims, 58 control studies, five plain answers (including whether a fly brain can learn), and our own tests: against an activity-matched control, the two sides disagree about the relays, and we do not draw a conclusion (brain only, one model; not a real fly).

summary: 152 entries checked on 15 Oct 2026 (8 new in the seventeenth check: flyscore A (helps), flybrain-prove-ai A (mixed; the AUW160150/flybrain mirror at the same commit is named in the record), flylab-pharmacology A (not scored: no better or worse direction), malecns-training-gomoku A (no difference), fly-connectome-study A (mixed), flylab-demo C, discord-fly-brain C and roblox-fly-avatar-claim U (a claim from a recap video; builder unknown, video not watched, no code); project claims are the projects' own, not ours; NeuroPest and FlyGift are linked by their source repositories only): 41 grade A, 38 B, 34 C, 4 D, 10 U and 25 datasets, tools or engines (not graded). trained_class: 69 of 117 graded projects have a trained, learning or search-tuned part in the main path, 48 have none. Re-graded from code (15 Oct 2026): the Pokémon-on-a-Raspberry-Pi stream (fly-pokemon-pi5-stream) U to B, borderline C: its code (ianwes92/fly-brain-plays-pokemon) runs the whole FlyWire FAFB v783 graph as a leaky integrate-and-fire network; game RAM is mapped to visual neurons; a hand-written priority arbiter turns descending-neuron rates into keys; chat keys and a paid override can replace the fly's keys; only Kenyon-cell to MBON synapses learn; no shuffled-wiring control; we did not watch the stream. Owner move (13 Oct 2026): chessfly and fly67 moved from github.com/znatgost to github.com/gexhaw; their try and source links follow.

Our flyvis layout test (made by us, pre-registered; tried on 10 and 12 Oct 2026): Not decided: a second, lower-memory attempt on 12 Oct also needed more memory than our shared machine has (about 3 GB at its peak; the machine allows 3 GB for everything running on it). Measured: it ran out while preparing the moving-edge test input, before the first simulation step (sampled peak about 3.17 GB of the 3.22 GB limit, which is 3 GiB). First attempt, 10 Oct 2026: Not decided: the test did not run, because it needed more memory than our shared machine has. A pre-registered setup check also failed, so no result would have been read. No result in either direction, no ledger row, no chart. We did not retrain the model after shuffling. A model trained on the shuffled wiring might do better, so this asks a narrower question: does this trained model depend on the real layout? The light-versus-dark (ON/OFF) test cannot tell real from shuffled wiring here: the shuffle keeps each connection's sign and total strength, and the authors report that signs alone are enough for it. Model: flyvis (MIT), Lappalainen et al. 2024, PMC11525180, commit 92b3845c.

The relays against an activity-matched control (made by us, brain only, pre-registered at 10:18 UTC on 13 Oct 2026 before the first trial): The two sides disagree: on one side silencing the relays lowered the turn neuron's rate more than matched activity elsewhere, on the other it did not. We do not draw a conclusion. 15 Oct: we ran 5 more matched controls on the right side, 10 in all. Every one of them left the turn neuron's rate higher than silencing the relays did (controls 38-47 Hz, relays 25.7 Hz), so the right-side reading did not change. Our rule compares the relays with the lowest matched control, so extra controls can only make the relays look less special, never more. Left eye: nothing silenced 21-25 Hz, matched control 13-34 Hz, relays E2 16.0 Hz (fell, like matched activity), PVLP141 alone 17.7 Hz. Right eye: 40-49 Hz, 40-43 Hz, E2 25.7 Hz (fell more than matched activity), PVLP141 alone 27.0 Hz. The control silences other neurons matched one by one on activity (within 20% of each relay neuron's spike count); the 9 Oct random control removed 2-6 times as much activity (2.3 times left, 5.8 times right). 5 seeds per side; 5 matched draws on the left and 10 on the right, 3 relay seeds; some matched draws include neurons that connect directly to the turn neuron; E2 is mostly PVLP141; a brain-only simulated rate, not fly behaviour.

The looming turn in degrees, at each input strength (made by us, pre-registered at 09:28 UTC on 14 Oct 2026; a simulated FlyGym body steered by the brain model; every brain drive that differs from the no-brain floor now has a body run). Left eye: In the body, the fly turned away from 30 spikes/s per looming neuron upward on this side, the strength at which the brain's turn command appeared; the turn was about 11 deg at 30 and about 37 deg at 80 (our mapping turns the brain's rates into steering). Right eye: At 30 spikes/s the turn was borderline: the fly turned away in 1 of 2 runs on this side; from 40 upward it turned away in every run. The right-eye borderline rests on one run: seed 0 at 30 spikes/s turned 9.18 deg beyond the no-brain floor, against the 10 deg rule. These body runs turn the brain's firing rates into steering through our own hand-made mapping, so they show the brain result in degrees; they are not a separate test of the wiring. No scrambled brains were run at these strengths. Seed 2 at 30, 40, 60 and 80 spikes/s: left 11.1, 27.2, 26.9, 37.2 deg, right 16.8, 33.8, 62.2, 55.4 deg (the turn did not grow at every step); one body run per drive.

Body lines under the 13 Oct relay headline (14 Oct 2026, descriptive, one run per arm and side, shadow at 80 spikes/s; the headline stays: the two sides disagree and we do not draw a conclusion): left eye: With PVLP141 silenced, the fly still turned away, by about 24 deg instead of 37 deg (one run per side; our mapping). With all 21-23 two-step relay neurons silenced, the fly still turned away, by about 37 deg instead of 37 deg (one run per side; our mapping). (unrounded 37.3 vs 37.2 deg) right eye: With PVLP141 silenced, the fly still turned away, by about 34 deg instead of 55 deg (one run per side; our mapping). With all 21-23 two-step relay neurons silenced, the fly still turned away, by about 40 deg instead of 55 deg (one run per side; our mapping). These body runs turn the brain's firing rates into steering through our own hand-made mapping, so they show the brain result in degrees; they are not a separate test of the wiring. No scrambled brains were run at these strengths.

Which relays carry the turn? Read by firing rate (made by us, brain only, pre-registered at 09:36:50 UTC on 9 Oct 2026 before the first trial; 30 runs): silencing the relays lowered the turn command to about 60-70% of normal, but silencing random active neurons also moved it, so this is not yet specific to the relays. Silencing other active neurons also changed the turn command, so this relay result is not specific to the relay neurons. With one relay neuron (PVLP141) silenced, the turn command fell to about 70% (left eye) / 65% (right eye) of normal (3 runs per eye). With the 17 (left eye) / 20 (right eye) relay neurons that excite the turn neuron silenced, the turn command fell to about 65% (left eye) / 60% (right eye) of normal (3 runs per eye). The left eye's normal range is only 1 Hz wide (24-25 Hz, three runs) and the random control is one draw per eye. One model (Shiu et al. LIF on FlyWire v783), brain only; the input is a rate we set for every LC4/LPLC2 of one eye, not a measured response to a real shadow; 'silenced' means the neuron's output synapses were removed; the normal range comes from 3 runs per eye; not a real fly. The 8 Oct relay sentences hold only with their label "by the left/right contrast (8 Oct)". Note added 13 Oct 2026: the random control behind this 9 Oct summary removed 2-6 times as much activity as the relays; see the activity-matched test of 13 Oct.

What the map leaves out (9 Oct 2026, How it works): The model is one fly's wiring map: 138,639 neurons and 15,091,983 connections, run with one simple neuron rule. It leaves out electrical synapses (gap junctions), neuropeptides, learning, the different behaviour of different kinds of neurons (including neurons that do not spike), the differences between flies and over a fly's life, and the nerve cord and body. So it can show what the wiring alone does, not everything a fly's brain does. Eight parts, one number and one source each: 0 electrical links (8 innexin genes in the fly); 8,316 neuromodulator neurons wired in as fast excitatory connections; more than 50 neuropeptide precursors, none in the model; fixed weights (synapse count x 0.275 mV); 1 neuron rule for 138,639 neurons; transmitters predicted at 94% per neuron; 53% of connections found again in a second fly; about 20,000 nerve-cord neurons absent. No total share is given: the rows measure different things.

How strong must the shadow be? (made by us, brain only, pre-registered at 09:45:48 UTC on 8 Oct 2026 before the first trial; 19 trials): We lowered the input to the looming neurons step by step, from 80 to 10 spikes per second each. The turn command appeared from about 30 per second (38% of our strongest input) on both sides; below that the model did not turn. The escape neuron started firing at the same input as the turn command. Reading: "moderate"; escape order "together"; a second seed agreed ("stable across seeds"). With one relay neuron (PVLP141) silenced, the turn command stayed (by the left/right contrast (8 Oct)). With all 21-23 relay neurons between the looming neurons and the turn neuron silenced, the turn command stayed (by the left/right contrast (8 Oct)). 'Stayed' means the pre-registered turn rule still passed; the ratio we used saturates because the near-side turn neuron is always at 0 Hz, and with PVLP141 silenced the far-side turn-neuron rate did fall (left 25 to 17 Hz, right 41 to 24 Hz); a disclosure, not a new reading. One model (Shiu et al. LIF on FlyWire v783), brain only; the input is a rate we set for every LC4/LPLC2 of one eye, not a measured response to a real shadow; 'silenced' means the neuron's output synapses were removed; not a real fly. We found no measured real-fly LC4/LPLC2 rate to compare against.

Where in the wiring is the turn? (6 Oct 2026; made by us, brain only, pre-registered at 09:42:54 UTC on 6 Oct 2026 before the first trial; 22 new trials with a faster input that passed its pre-registered check): We turned the scrambled maps up until they were as busy as the real one. They still did not produce the turn: the wiring, not the amount of activity, makes it. 3 of 3 shuffles matched the real activity (gain 2.25, 0.98 x real outside the stimulated cells) and all gave a 0 Hz turn command. Inside-only scramble: Scrambling only the inside of the map kept about -9% of the turn command and 69% of the escape signal. (-9% means none: the far-side command was absent in all 6 trials; descriptive, not pre-registered: the near-side giant fibre kept 151-169 Hz, the far side went to 0). With the escape neuron silenced, the turn command stayed. (2 of 2; expected, as the map has no giant fibre to DNa02 connections). Census: no direct looming-to-DNa02 synapses; top relay PVLP141. Brain only: 7 drives await body runs.

We ran the map (5 and 8 Oct 2026, pre-registered): We ran the map. A looming shadow on one eye turned our simulated fly away in 6 of 6 runs. With the same map scrambled (same number of connections per neuron) it turned away in 0 of 3. Here the map's wiring, not the stimulus or our code, makes the turn. Left eye 3 of 3, right eye 3 of 3; the 5 Oct floor run repeated exactly on 8 Oct. With the escape neuron silenced, the fly still turned away (2 of 2). With only the inside of the map scrambled, the fly turned away in 0 of 6 runs. One model, open loop, our hand-made mapping, a constant external walking drive, 1 s; the body walks with FlyGym's controller; not a real fly. fly67 stays grade B.

Can a fly brain learn maths, to hack or to play a game? (13 Oct 2026, our reading of 13 projects; each claim is the project's own): Some projects say so. By our reading of 13 of them, practice changes a trained readout (3), trained settings across the network (4) or a learning rule on some connections (3); 1 trains nothing; 2 give no code. 3 compare with scrambled wiring.

Plain answers with evidence on Is it real?: Is it AI? (the base model is not trained AI; 69 of 117 graded projects add trained, learning or tuned parts); Is it a brain or just a map? (a map run with a simple model; in our tests its wiring drove a reflex and a turn, body software did the walking); Is the fly being tortured? Can it suffer? (no study measured suffering in these models; whether flies feel pain is open); Can I put it in my game? (yes for non-commercial projects with credit, our cautious reading of CC BY-NC 4.0; not legal advice); What do I have to download? (two files, 104.1 MB, for the beginner path); new on 13 Oct: Can a fly brain learn maths, to hack or to play a game? (some projects say so; by our reading practice changes a readout, settings across the network or some connections, each claim attributed to its project).

Controls ledger (15 Oct 2026): 58 studies, 49 with a wiring null: helps 22, no difference 11, worse 4, mixed 10, not yet scored 2. Five rows joined on 15 Oct, scored only by our fixed rules from the authors' own numbers (not recomputed by us): flyscore helps (sugar to MN9: real 1.0 over 40 trials vs 0.0 for 5 weight-shuffled and 5 rewired copies), flybrain-prove-ai mixed (connectome language model, bits per byte, lower is better: fly 2.6388 vs degree-rewired 2.6286, random graph 2.5827, GRU 2.5575), malecns-training-gomoku no difference (held-out tactical accuracy: fly 0.787 vs rewired 0.785, RNN 0.788, GRU 0.790), fly-connectome-study mixed (pre-registered foraging test, 200 worlds: real 44.0 vs shuffled 44.36, random 50.905, linear 46.17) and flylab-pharmacology not scored (imidacloprid effect: real -0.678 Hz vs rewired -0.267, weight permutation -1.102, random -0.974, sign permutation -0.379; the metric has no better or worse direction). No scoring rule changed. Earlier: Three rows joined on 13 Oct, scored only by our fixed rules from the authors' own numbers (not recomputed by us): malecns-visual-motor helps (DNp15 contrast +81.2 Hz vs -3.4, +1.4 and -0.2 Hz for 3 rewired graphs; partly fair, strong), malecns-keratitis-pilot no difference (AUROC 0.479 vs 0.464 for 10 rewired, paired interval -0.037 to +0.064; fair, strong; a negative result reported by its author) and fly-brain-sim helps (giant fibre 163-177 Hz vs 47-73 Hz shuffled strengths and 0 Hz scrambled targets; partly fair, weak; lab-notebook ranges). No scoring rule changed. One row joined on 12 Oct (duth-x-stepmania helps) and five on 11 Oct.
Our walking test (2 Oct): real brain 13.93 mm, scrambled 14.15 mm, brainless constant drive 14.28 mm in 1 s; the legs are FlyGym's, and our mapping capped the drive.

Our 1 Oct reflex test on the sugar reflex: real wiring 85.2 ± 3.56 Hz; degree-preserving and weight shuffles 0 Hz; boundary-preserving 39 Hz (retention 0.46); sign shuffle 214 Hz with the whole brain ignited. The gain-matched arm was not matched on 3 shuffles; the row stays mixed, unfair and weak.

Where the wiring helps, a brain-free baseline often matches the fly anyway: the fly network beats a no-brain baseline in only 4 of 27 studies. In Doom (doom-fly-control by gabrycina) the fly survives 53.34 s, shuffled wiring 6.75 s and a brainless autopilot 51.93 s.

Build your own: tested 28 Sep 2026 on Linux with 2 CPUs (MN9 85.2 Hz real, 0 Hz shuffled) and re-tested 5 Oct 2026 (6 of 6 tests, 82.0 Hz bit-exact). Tested deeper steps: Add a body (2 Oct, FlyGym 2.1.0, our mapping), Add a sense: looming (5 Oct), and brain and body in one Python 3.12 environment (8 Oct: 1.1 GB on disk, numpy pinned to 2.3.5; with numpy 2.5.3, import brian2 fails with AttributeError: type object 'numpy.ndarray' has no attribute 'ptp'). Use in class: a 20-minute plan with play.drosophila.io as an alternative.

Does it actually run? (our browser checks of 3, 6 and 11 Oct 2026, headless Chromium 154, Linux, no GPU; not a play test): 9 of 12 demos ran. 11 Oct: fly-arithmetic's website ran with no action from us (first activity after about 11.2 s, about 2.05 MB; where it computes could not be told; we did not type a sum). 6 Oct: Vial 7.43 MB, Doodle Fly 34.99 MB and Infinite Sugar 36.04 MB ran computing in your browser, Fly Dino 3.81 MB ran, and Neural Canvas ran but its ~77 MB brain download was not seen in our check window. 3 Oct: Fly Worker, FLY67 and flybrain.app ran; FlyLeno and Help the Fly Escape froze after loading; fly-brain (Lulzx) stopped at our 1.6 GB memory limit. No demo computed on a server.

New entries (15 Oct 2026): flyscore (A), flybrain-prove-ai (A), flylab-pharmacology (A), malecns-training-gomoku (A) and fly-connectome-study (A) each compare the real wiring with scrambled or rewired copies (ledger rows above); flylab-demo (C), discord-fly-brain (C, hand-designed weights) and roblox-fly-avatar-claim (U) do not. New entries (14 Oct 2026): fly-cx-navigation-servo (B), NeuroPest (B, source repository only), Fly Garden (B) and FastBrain (n/a, a simulator speed-up); none compares the real wiring with a scrambled copy. New entries (13 Oct 2026): malecns-visual-motor (A, helps in its own rewired comparison), malecns-keratitis-pilot (A, no difference, a negative result), fly-chess (B), adfly-connectome (B), fly-brain-sim (B) and FlyGift (B, source repository only). New entries (12 Oct 2026): duth-x-stepmania (A, with its own rewired-circuit control) and flyonenomics (B, spiking activity only, no wiring control). New entries (11 Oct 2026): MelanoGraph (A), fly-arithmetic (A), FlyRoyale (B) and connectome-control-exploration (B). New entries (9 Oct 2026): FlyVL (A), Flappy Fly (B), FlyWire Playground (B) and Let It Flyppen (C).

"Can A Conscious Fly Brain Learn how to Hack?" by dzuma (approximately 72,728 views on 12 Oct 2026, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m5Q_aIO_K8o): no code linked, grade U. "I Taught a Fly How to Play Gorilla Tag (seriously)" (approximately 1,005,369 views on 12 Oct 2026, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wK4lixw7p4M) still names no code: U. The 12 Oct lead scan promoted no new claim.

Video gallery (checked 15 Oct 2026: 56 of 56 videos available; view counts keep their own dates): view counts of 15 cards refreshed on 12 Oct 2026 from search pages, for example FlyLeno's playthrough video approximately 53,325 views on 12 Oct 2026. The DOOMFLY announcement card no longer says its read-out cells were chosen because they responded to the screen (not in the cited files). View counts are approximate snapshots with their date. Thumbnails unchanged.

Download facts (6 Oct 2026, from hosts' storage metadata, no data downloaded): the beginner path needs Connectivity_783.parquet (100,804,642 B) and Completeness_783.csv (3,327,347 B); FlyWire v783 on Zenodo 10.6 GB in 5 files, MaleCNS v1.0 31.3 GB in 11 files, BANC 536.1 GB in 379 files (308.3 GB on request). MANC and larva L1 sizes are not stated.
"91%" is the share of 164 testable predictions of the brain-only Shiu et al. 2024 model that matched experiments; "95%" compares versions of the model and is not an accuracy.
FlyWire data is CC BY-NC 4.0 in FlyWire's guidelines (non-commercial; the Zenodo v783 record says CC BY 4.0, and we follow the stricter reading); MaleCNS, MANC, hemibrain and BANC data are CC BY.
uncertainty: Our looming tests: one model (Shiu et al. LIF on FlyWire v783), our hand-made mapping, an input we set (every LC4 and LPLC2 of one eye at a fixed rate for 1 s); not a real fly. Body (5 and 8 Oct): 6 real runs and 3 scrambled body runs with identical drives; 3 more scrambled and 5 inside-only drives equal the no-brain floor and take its walk by determinism (the floor run repeated exactly). Brain only (6 Oct): n 6 real, 6 plain scramble, 3 turned-up scramble, 6 inside-only, 2 giant fibre off. Brain only (8 Oct): one input series per eye (seed 2) and 4 second-seed checks; the 8 Oct relay readings rest on a ratio that saturates when the near side is silent. Brain only (9 Oct, relays by firing rate): the normal range comes from 3 runs per eye and is only 1 Hz wide on the left (24-25 Hz); the random-neuron control is one draw and one seed per eye, so the summary is "not specific to the relay neurons"; no measured real-fly LC4/LPLC2 rate was found to compare with. The 'away' direction rests on our mapping's DNa02 sign and fly67's claim.

Body runs at each input strength (14 Oct 2026): one body run per drive (seed 2 at every strength, seed 0 only at 20 and 30 spikes/s); the right-eye borderline turns on one run 0.8 deg under the 10 deg rule; the degrees come from our own hand-made mapping from turning-neuron rates to steering with a walking drive we hold constant, so they restate the brain result and are not a separate test of the wiring; no scrambled brains were run at these strengths; the relay body lines are one run per arm and side.

Relays against an activity-matched control (13 Oct 2026): 5 seeds per side; 5 matched draws on the left and 10 on the right (5 added on 15 Oct 2026), and 3 relay seeds; the left matched draws spread widely (13-34 Hz); some matched draws include neurons that synapse directly onto the far-side turn neuron (1 of 5 left, 2 of 10 right; none of the 5 added on 15 Oct); E2 is mostly PVLP141 (102 of 149 and 103 of 121 removed spikes), so the test says little about the other relay neurons. Our rule compares the relays with the lowest matched control, so extra controls can only make the relays look less special, never more. One model, brain only, a simulated rate, not fly behaviour.

Can it learn?: the classes are our reading of each project's code or README at one commit; the two video-only records are not checked; a shuffled-wiring comparison reported by an author was not re-run by us.

What the map leaves out: each number comes from one page read on 9 Oct 2026 or from our own model files; the neuropeptide count is a review's statement; the innexin and Nature pages answered bot checks, so PubMed Central copies (one via NCBI E-utilities) were read. The rows measure different things, so there is no total share missing.

The plain answers rest on our reading of project files (trained_class), one primary nociception source, hosts' storage metadata for download sizes and our licence reading, which is not legal advice; whether CC BY or CC BY-NC applies to a FlyWire release is an open question with FlyWire.

Our body test covers one stimulus (P9 at 150 Hz on both sides), one brain model, one body, 1 s of open-loop walking, 3 trial seeds and 3 shuffles that sent identical drives. The rate-to-drive mapping is ours: it caps the drive at 1.2, so another mapping could let the wiring matter more. The pre-registered P9 sign, other P9 rates and other descending neuron types were not tested in the body.

Our reflex test covers one reflex (sugar to MN9) in one model, with one 1 s trial per shuffle at one trial seed; the MN9 rate cannot tell selective drive from global ignition. The gain-matched arm is not matched on 3 shuffles; a per-shuffle gain search has not been run.

Browser checks (3 and 6 Oct): one headless Chromium 154 on Linux without a GPU, 60-90 s per demo, one action each; not a play test. Both freezes most likely come from software WebGL on our machine; GPU machines, Safari, Firefox and phones were not tested. Activity detection is coarse (screenshots every 5 s), bytes cover only the first 60-90 s, and traffic in cross-origin frames is not counted. Protocol completions and three deviations (a tool bug fixed and re-run within the 2-load limit) were written down but not pre-registered by the planner. View counts come from YouTube search pages; the Terraria, Gorilla Tag and Roblox fight videos were not watched. Neural Canvas's ~77 MB brain download was not seen in our 6 Oct window; where Fly Dino and Neural Canvas compute is unclear by our fixed rule.
The Terraria verdict rests on code older than the video; fly-walking-wiring's B is provisional because its results are not public. The Flyhard match of the driving compilation rests on one thumbnail.

Controls ledger: every number except our own three tests is the authors'. We recomputed 18 studies from their committed files but re-ran none; none is replicated, and only 2 of 58 are peer-reviewed. Only 22 of 58 studies reach "strong" method quality; 27 are weak. Fly-Racer and FlyBrain Flappy rest on README numbers; fly tennis rests on one match per condition. Synaptera's class follows the fixed rules; we did not inspect its shuffle method. Connectocopter's baseline arm is read from its README. FlyVL's numbers are the author's committed result files, not recomputed by us; a rerun of the same harness gave a smaller gap (+0.111). The five rows of 11 Oct use the authors' numbers: fly-distill, MelanoGraph and the mushroom-body model rest on author summaries; MelanoGraph and brainlab each rest on one rewired graph (weak). duth-x-stepmania (12 Oct) rests on one seed and the mean of 3 rewired copies, and its readout groups come from the real wiring. fly-brain-sim (13 Oct) rests on ranges in a lab notebook, scored at their midpoints; malecns-keratitis-pilot uses private clinical data, so it could not be recomputed.

Ledger labels (wiring effect, fairness, quality) come from fixed yes/no rules applied to code and files; they are consistent but coarse. Our body test scores strong although its 3 shuffles behaved as one; our reflex test is "mixed" by rule although its arms read silent, partly and runaway. We did not override the rules for our own rows. Activity fields are reported only for our two tests. Retention puts very different measurements on one scale. The flyvis ablation values exist only in a figure and were not extracted; our text search of its supplement was crude (no PDF tool).

The "helps" results are mostly one kind of test (does a reflex pathway still carry signal after rewiring?), which is a low bar; boundary-preserving nulls have been applied to one reflex (ours: 46% kept), not to the other reflex studies.

Borderline grades: FlyLeno (B, borderline C); Fly Worker, fly-brain by Lulzx, The Fly's Hash Function, Fly OCR, Fly Self Driving, the null-model study and fly-brain-zero-shot are borderline A; fly-brain by erojas and Kick the Fly could argue B; acamilo-flybrain would sit on the B/C border without its stream macros.

Several C grades and the fafbseg entry rest on file citations that we spot-read but did not re-verify line by line. fly-plays-games runs its neurons in an external package (fly.ai) that we did not inspect beyond its commit subjects.

The Rainbow Six claim is known only through news articles and search summaries; the Pokémon stream's grade (B, borderline C) rests on its public code at one commit, not on watching the stream; the Roblox avatar claim rests on a recap video's description (builder unknown, video not watched). X, TikTok and Reddit cannot be searched without a login.

Not yet triaged in code: 3 priority-1 leads whose READMEs describe a control (adfly-connectome, malecns-visual-motor, malecns-keratitis-pilot), 11 lower-priority leads, 5 new GitHub leads of 12 Oct, and about 211 repositories listed only in directories. Two exclusions of 12 Oct rest only on a missing README.md.

Why the Shiu v783 file has 616 fewer neurons than the FlyWire v783 release is not established; the scope of BANC's "approximately 188,000 neurons" is not stated. The attractor reported for the Shiu et al. model has not been reproduced by us.

The Build your own guide is untested on macOS, Windows/WSL, Colab and machines with a C++ compiler; GitHub Pages publishing is untested. Add a body is tested on Linux CPU only, without rendering. DOOMFLY's and DesktopFly's run steps are untested by us.
FlyWire data licence conflict: CC BY-NC 4.0 in the official guidelines vs CC BY 4.0 on the Zenodo v783 record; we follow the stricter, non-commercial reading.
Video summaries rest on titles, descriptions, captions, code and thumbnails; we did not watch every video frame by frame. View counts are snapshots.

Videos cannot play inside the site: YouTube, Vimeo, TikTok and X players failed in the site's sandboxed frames (tested in headless Chromium only). YouTube and X thumbnails are loaded from their image servers.

Download facts: sizes are the hosts' own storage figures on 6 Oct 2026; MANC (bucket not listed) and larva L1 (supplement unreachable) sizes are not stated; the FlyWire Codex download page needs a sign-in and was not read; the hemibrain flat file is v1.2 while neuPrint serves v1.2.1.
Our environment test: one Linux machine, Python 3.12.11; Brian2 2.10.x with numpy 2.5 was not tested. A coupled brain-and-body test is not yet tested.

Our flyvis layout test has no result (stopped for memory on 10 and 12 Oct 2026), so nothing can be said about whether the real wiring layout matters for motion direction in that model. The lower-memory loop itself was never measured; that building the test input caused the memory jump is a reading of the timing, not a profile. Even a run that works would ask only whether the trained model depends on the real layout, because the model is not trained again after shuffling.
